thread.title_full: Firefighters winning war against Big Rock Fire near Heise - NewsBreak

author: Post Register Staff
title: Firefighters winning war against Big Rock Fire near Heise - NewsBreak
text:
By Post Register Staff ,
6 hours ago
Firefighters battling the Big Rock Fire notched their biggest win yet this week, reaching 22% containment Tuesday night of a blaze that at times seemed unstoppable.
It's the first containment percentage reported since the lightning-caused wildfire exploded to life last Friday near Heise, a community northeast of Idaho Falls.
The milestone caps a steady turnaround for crews who spent the fire's first days purely on defense. The fire's size has held essentially flat at 2,199 acres, a slight dip from the previously reported 2,204 acres reflecting more accurate mapping rather than any renewed growth.
The fire's perimeter has not changed since Monday morning thanks to the efforts of firefighters as well as cooler and calmer weather conditions at the scene.
Fire crews have also gotten reinforcements to match their momentum. The number of personnel assigned to the fire has grown to 278, up from roughly 250 earlier in the week and more than double the 126 firefighters who held the line during the fire's most dangerous days this past weekend.
Fire crews have achieved partial containment on the fire's northern flank above Cress Creek, a sign of the progress being made across the burn. Wednesday's plans call for widening containment lines on the hill north of Kelly Canyon and state endowment lands to the north, securing South Snake River Road and Heise Road, pushing further uphill to clear hazard trees, and extinguishing hotspots deeper in the fire's interior.
Active fire activity has continued to decrease, officials said, even as pockets of heat and smoldering material, including the occasional torching juniper, remain scattered across the burned area. One helicopter was assigned Wednesday afternoon to assist with water bucket drops, and crews were inspecting the Cress Creek trail to clear hazards and assess repair needs.
After Monday saw the first signs that the tide was turning at the fire scene, Tuesday brought more of the same steady progress: crews added depth and support to containment lines throughout the day, with engines backing up hand crews working inward from the fire's perimeter to remove heat and extinguish smoldering vegetation. Crews made good headway constructing a mastication containment line along Forest Road 218 and continued work in the Cress Creek area, while helicopters spent the day dousing junipers that continued to torch.
Favorable weather has been on firefighters' side since Monday. Tuesday brought sunny skies, temperatures ranging from the upper 70s to mid-80s and west-northwest winds generally 5 to 10 mph. Wednesday's conditions had more of the same — sunny skies, temperatures in the low to mid-80s, humidity below 20% and light winds — with no rain expected but also no repeat of the extreme heat and gusts that fueled the fire's explosive early growth.
Officials noted that even with the improved outlook, there's still real work ahead. Steep, inaccessible terrain continues to challenge crews, and rocks and burning material have been rolling downhill toward roads and structures, a hazard crews are continuing to monitor closely as they push containment lines forward.
There have still been no injuries to firefighters or the public, and no residences have been lost — the fire's toll remains limited to two unused sheds destroyed over the weekend.
Evacuation orders have continued to ease alongside the fire's improving status. Madison County has moved the South Snake River Road evacuation area from "Go" to "Ready" status, allowing residents and property owners in that area to pass road closures to check on their properties.
All other roads remain closed to the public and authorities are still urging people to stay away from the fire scene.
Recreation restrictions have begun to ease in another sign of the progress being made. The Bureau of Land Management announced Wednesday afternoon it has lifted the closure on river camping at designated sites within the South Fork of the Snake River Canyon between the Conant and Byington boat accesses.
Camping closures remain in effect at Kelly Island Campground, Wolf Flats, Warm Springs and all dispersed sites along River Road, which BLM said are necessary to protect firefighters traveling the Heise/South Snake River Road.
Closures also remain in place on the Cress Creek Nature Trail, Stinking Springs Trail and all other hiking and biking trails in the Kelly Canyon and Heise areas. The temporary closures were put in place at the fire's onset and are set to expire at 11:59 p.m. Aug. 10 unless extended.
Caribou-Targhee National Forest and Idaho Department of Lands closures tied to the fire remain in effect as well.
Fire officials once again credited the successful response to fire departments, sheriff's offices and emergency management personnel in Bonneville, Jefferson and Madison counties, who stepped up as federal resources were stretched thin by catastrophic fires burning across the West.
